narrativeProgression.description: Sabine introduces herself and her expertise in hyperspectral remote sensing.
She explains her role in the EnMAP project, a German hyperspectral satellite mission.
She details the EnMAP PI project, its focus on data exploitation, and the availability of free data and software.
Sabine discusses the advantages of spaceborne hyperspectral imaging, particularly for understanding soil degradation and composition.
She presents several examples of scientific studies using hyperspectral data, highlighting the technique's capabilities in different applications.
Sabine expands on the wide range of potential users for hyperspectral data and products.
She addresses current challenges, including data interpretation and lack of trained personnel, emphasizing the need for educational programs like Hyperedu.

text_to_speech: "Our first stop is the German Research Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam, located on the Telegrafenberg in a historic science campus surrounded by forest. At the GFZ scientists study the dynamics of planet Earth, not just the solid Earth and the surface on which we live, but also the hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere. And the chemical, physical, and biological processes that connect them. Among others, Earth observation is a key technique for understanding the Earth. It has a long tradition here on Telegrafenberg. Besides the GFZ, there are other research centres here on campus, such as the Alfred Wegener Institute for Polar and Marine Research and the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, as well as historic buildings like the famous Einstein Tower. For our first expert interview, we will meet very close to the Einstein Tower." PROF. DR. SABINE CHABRILLAT: I'm a specialist in hyperspectral remote sensing and have been working in this field for the past 25 years now. And especially I'm a specialist in soil spectroscopy and digital soil mapping. We are part of a section remote sensing and geoinformatics. And we are actually pioneers in the field. We have been working on advanced optical remote sensing, sensor definition and also new methodologies for the past 25 years now. And nowadays, we are one of the key players internationally. So in 2003, this is our section under the lead of Charlie Kaufman, who was the head of a section at that time, we proposed there was a DLR announcement of opportunity for German national missions. And we were the ones who proposed a hyperspectral satellite. This mission is now funded. So nowadays we are the head of the science segment of the satellite. We are coordinating the EnMAP science and advisory group. We are coordinating the EnMAP PI project, which is a project to support science development and algorithms, developments for the exploitation of EnMAP data. So this is a national consortium with four partners in Germany. So in the phase from 2020 to 2023, we are covering the pre-launch phase, the commissioning phase and the start of a nominal phase. And this is focusing on the mission preparation for the exploitation of the data and support to DLR. In particular, some focus in this current phase are the development also of educational tools like the HYPERedu platform, some flight campaigns and some algorithms developments in the EnMAP-Box. Another area of development is free-and-open data and free-and-open software. So the EnMAP data will be offered for free for the user community and software are available for free also. Right now in the context of big, climatic and anthropogenic changes with lots of soil degradation, and hyperspectral remote sensing technique is something that can really help in characterising on terms of quantifications for composition of a soils. Spaceborne hyperspectral remote sensing is very interesting, because in the difference of field or laboratory data that are available only in a test case study and also field and laboratory data are very costly, you need to organise a team going there, it takes time, it takes lots of instrument. So the spaceborne allow to have a repetition of acquisition of data. And so, you can do also monitoring of earth surface processes and mapping some changes at the surface linked to anthropogenic and climate changes. So the advantage of the hyperspectral remote sensing technique compared to multispectral is that we have access to the diagnostic signal but is really characteristics of the minerals of the surface. For example, we can directly from looking at the physical signals received by a satellite, we can directly identify: Is this a calcite? Is it iron? Is it clay? Is there some organic carbon content? So all this are really diagnostic from the signal. And this is something that only the hyperspectral technique can provide. Yeah, for example, we had a very nice demonstration scientific work that was based in southern Spain, so in the Cabo de Gata Natural Park. It’s an agricultural area, it's an iron-rich soil and in this area, thanks to hyperspectral remote sensing, we were able to simulate upcoming EnMAP images. And we could also simulate upcoming EnMAP products in terms of iron oxides content map, and also clay content, which is very nice, because it delineates the areas with more soil moisture and more fertility. And in another science study, we are working in the TERENO long term observatory in northern Germany. So the name of a test area is Demmin. And in this area we have a very high variability in organic carbon at the top soils at the surface of the soils. And in this area, we were able to simulate EnMAP imagery also, and to develop new tools and to map soil organic carbon content on the surface. So in another science issue, we looked at the impact of hyperspectral remote sensing to map raw materials at the surface and in the mining environment. So this is a study with testsites in Namibia and North and South Africa. And there they were able to do a very nice simulation of EnMAP products with identifying the different geological minerals. So, this is really a very nice study, because it shows that in such an arid environment and also it's an area it’s a very rugged terrain, well normally for geologists is very hard to access, you can now develop such products. So the range of users is endless, includes NGOs, governmental institutions, public authorities, individual farmers like individual people, so the user groups are very endless and very wide. Current challenges now are in the exploitation of the data, because there are still some methodologies that involve big data, data science, machine learning and artificial intelligence that are now in full developments. And those new methods will be very useful to extract the complexity inside the hyperspectral data. And important avenue of development and current challenge now is that the community is still not trained to use or to know the potential of this data. And we have to develop big educational program such as the MOOC here or such as HYPERedu. And there are such educational programs also internationally that are in developments so that the users really learn how useful is the data and how they can process it.

youtube_description:
What is the actual benefit of hyperspectral data? Hear what Prof. Dr. Sabine Chabrillat (professor for “digital soil mapping” at Leibniz University Hanover, Institute of Soil Sciences, German Research Centre for Geosciences – GFZ in Potsdam and Principal Investigator of the EnMAP satellite mission) thinks about the advantages of hyperspectral imagery and current challenges for imaging spectroscopy in the context of soils and geology.

**** FREE ONLINE COURSE ****

‘Beyond the Visible – Introduction to Hyperspectral Remote Sensing‘ is the first Massive Open Online Course (MOOC) on Hyperspectral Remote Sensing presented by HYPERedu and EO-College
 
OPEN FROM 24 NOVEMBER 2021, 08:00 am GMT 

Register now: https://eo-college.org/courses/beyond-the-visible/

The course teaches the principles of imaging spectroscopy, sensor technologies and data acquisition techniques, hyperspectral data processing approaches and data sources and provides expert-guided hands-on training. 

The course was developed by GFZ Potsdam as part of the HYPERedu initiative with support from experts at various partner institutions. The development was funded within the EnMAP science program under the German Space Agency at DLR with resources from the German Federal Ministry of Economic Affairs and Energy.

**** For FURTHER INFORMATION we recommend ****
